title: Michigan Judicial Ethics Opinion JI-155: judicial officers must maintain competence with AI (27 October 2023)
pub: State Bar of Michigan — Ethics Opinion JI-155
author: State Bar of Michigan Judicial Ethics Committee

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: JI-155 accepts the cluster’s core model of AI as supervised assistance and materially develops it by grounding continuing AI competence, lawful use and scrutiny in judicial ethical duties. It also sharpens the boundary between AI informing a decision and AI deciding, while requiring judges to retain and record their own reasoning.
qs: **CONCLUSION**  Judicial officers have an ethical obligation to understand technology, including artificial intelligence, and take reasonable steps to ensure that AI tools on which their judgment will be based are used properly and that the AI tools are utilized within the confines of the law and court rules.
Judicial use of AI must distinguish between using an AI application to decide and using AI to inform a decision.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: JI-155 accepts the cluster’s core principle of continuing human accountability and adds a concrete judicial-governance framework: judges must maintain AI competence, ensure lawful and proper use, and transparently place their own analysis and reasoning on the record. It also supports ongoing, tool-sensitive reassessment rather than blanket prohibition.
qs: **CONCLUSION**  Judicial officers have an ethical obligation to understand technology, including artificial intelligence, and take reasonable steps to ensure that AI tools on which their judgment will be based are used properly and that the AI tools are utilized within the confines of the law and court rules.
The most important thing courts can do today is to ask the right questions and place their analysis and application of how they reached their conclusion on the record.

st.t: Justice access: Direct AI use shifts risk downward
st.an: The opinion accepts that AI can benefit legal work when properly used and materially extends the cluster’s governance model with court-specific safeguards: attorney review, disclosure, accuracy confirmation and judicial responsibility for managing AI use. It does not directly assess unrepresented users or whether direct-to-consumer AI shifts risk downward.
qs: To ensure this, some courts[[4]](#_ftn4) have issued rulings or orders regarding the use of AI, such as requiring attorney review, placing the responsibility on lawyers to notify the court when using AI, and provide confirmation of the accuracy of the work done by the AI tool.
Judges must determine the best course of action for their courts with the ever-expanding use of AI.

st.t: Machine judging: Accuracy cannot establish legitimate authority
st.an: JI-155 accepts the cluster’s core distinction between AI assistance and delegated adjudication, and materially extends it by framing judicial AI competence as a continuing ethical duty. It adds concrete requirements for due-process scrutiny, tool-specific reassessment, accountable human reasoning and placing the court’s analysis on the record.
qs: Judicial use of AI must distinguish between using an AI application to decide and using AI to inform a decision.
The most important thing courts can do today is to ask the right questions and place their analysis and application of how they reached their conclusion on the record.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The opinion accepts the cluster’s human-led, selective-deployment model and materially extends it to judicial administration. It makes ongoing AI competence, tool-specific ethical assessment, verification and preservation of judicial judgment affirmative duties, while adding court-specific concerns such as impartiality, due process and transparent reasoning on the record.
qs: Judicial use of AI must distinguish between using an AI application to decide and using AI to inform a decision.
AI is becoming more advanced every day and is rapidly integrating within the judicial system, which requires continual thought and ethical assessment of the use, risks, and benefits of each tool.

st.t: Court governance: Assistive use retains human accountability
st.an: The opinion supports assistive AI use under continuing human accountability. It endorses attorney review, accuracy confirmation, disclosure and confidentiality safeguards, recognises properly used AI as beneficial, and stresses judicial competence and ongoing reassessment as systems evolve. Its practices are illustrative rather than uniform, consistent with the synthesis’s account of jurisdictional variation.
qs: To ensure this, some courts[[4]](#_ftn4) have issued rulings or orders regarding the use of AI, such as requiring attorney review, placing the responsibility on lawyers to notify the court when using AI, and provide confirmation of the accuracy of the work done by the AI tool.
Due to this learning capacity, AI applications may need to be re-litigated or re-evaluated on an ongoing basis, even when there is precedent addressing the same AI tool.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The opinion aligns with the cluster’s copilot framing: AI may benefit legal work when properly used, while lawyers and judges retain responsibility and courts may require human review, accuracy confirmation and disclosure. It also supports continuing reassessment as AI systems and uses evolve, though it does not address whether verification costs erase efficiency gains or whether grounding removes probabilistic error.
qs: To ensure this, some courts[[4]](#_ftn4) have issued rulings or orders regarding the use of AI, such as requiring attorney review, placing the responsibility on lawyers to notify the court when using AI, and provide confirmation of the accuracy of the work done by the AI tool.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The opinion directly supports the cluster’s supervised-aid framing: judges must understand AI’s risks, continually oversee its use, and remain accountable for judicial decisions rather than allowing AI to decide. It also supports continuing reassessment and context-specific verification or disclosure safeguards while recognising properly controlled efficiency benefits.
qs: **CONCLUSION**  Judicial officers have an ethical obligation to understand technology, including artificial intelligence, and take reasonable steps to ensure that AI tools on which their judgment will be based are used properly and that the AI tools are utilized within the confines of the law and court rules.
Judicial use of AI must distinguish between using an AI application to decide and using AI to inform a decision.

st.t: Supervisory accountability: Verification must test substantive support
st.an: The opinion supports retained human responsibility and court-level safeguards by emphasizing judicial scrutiny of cases and rules, attorney review, and confirmation of AI-output accuracy. It also treats AI competence as necessary for judges to select appropriate safeguards, though it does not develop a detailed standard for proportionate, source-level verification.

kp.k: Judicial technological competence includes continuing AI education
kp.d: The opinion interprets Michigan judicial ethics requirements as obliging judicial officers to understand advancing technology, including AI, and continue educating themselves. It connects this obligation to professional competence under Canon 3(A)(1) and judicial administration under Canon 3(B), alongside Michigan lawyers’ technological competence obligations under MRPC 1.1. Competence encompasses technologies used by judges, court staff and lawyers appearing before them.
qs: Judicial officers, like lawyers, have an ethical obligation to maintain competence with and further educate themselves on advancing technology, including but not limited to artificial intelligence (AI).
This includes knowing the benefits and risks associated with the technology that judicial officers and their staff use daily, as well as the technology used by lawyers who come before the bench.

kp.k: Algorithmic bias may compromise judicial fairness and impartiality
kp.d: The opinion identifies a conditional ethical risk, rather than a measured finding: biased algorithms or training data could influence judicial judgment and trigger Canons 2(B) and 2(C). AI might weigh legally or socially inappropriate factors, assign inappropriate weights, or produce results that disregard norms and precedent.
qs: Canon 2(B) and (C) could be triggered, for example, if a judicial officer uses an AI solution that is considered partial or unfair and may influence the judicial officer’s judgment.
This could occur if the tool’s algorithm or training data creates bias.
An algorithm may weigh factors that the law or society deem inappropriate or do so with a weight that is inappropriate in the context presented.

kp.k: Courts are imposing verification, disclosure and confidentiality safeguards
kp.d: Citing Mata v Avianca as an example of incorrect AI-generated filings, the opinion reports judicial concerns about verifying pleadings before relying on them. It describes orders from some courts requiring attorney review, AI-use disclosure and accuracy confirmation, and more extensive requirements from other judges concerning confidential information and identification of AI-generated sections. These are reported court practices, not a uniform requirement imposed by this opinion.
qs: As the legal community has seen, there are times when AI may be used improperly, i.e., when a lawyer submits AI-generated filings that are found to be incorrect.
To ensure this, some courts

have issued rulings or orders regarding the use of AI, such as requiring attorney review, placing the responsibility on lawyers to notify the court when using AI, and provide confirmation of the accuracy of the work done by the AI tool.
Other judges have gone further and required that attorneys certify that confidential information was not disseminated to an AI tool and that lawyers outline each section that uses generative AI.

kp.k: Proper AI use can support drafting, research and administration
kp.d: The opinion presents AI’s benefits as conditional on proper use: accurate pleadings and legal summaries, more efficient docket management and legal research, and algorithm-based answers. It leaves judges to determine the appropriate approach for their courts rather than prescribing blanket prohibition or adoption.
qs: However, there are times when, properly used, AI is an asset for the legal community, such as creating accurate content for pleadings and legal summaries, providing efficiency in docket management and legal research, and supplying answers to questions based on algorithms used by technological programs.
Judges must determine the best course of action for their courts with the ever-expanding use of AI.

kp.k: Evolving AI may require renewed litigation despite precedent
kp.d: The opinion predicts that advancing AI will become a subject of adjudication. It asserts that most AI programs continue learning and argues that resulting changes to algorithms and formulas may require ongoing re-litigation or re-evaluation even when precedent already addresses the same tool. This is a prospective rationale for continuing competence, not an empirical finding about litigation frequency.
qs: Advancing AI will eventually lead to inquiry and adjudication of AI-related technologies and their use in other matters before the court.
Most artificial intelligence programs continue to learn, which requires adjustments in algorithms and formulas as they receive new and additional data.
Due to this learning capacity, AI applications may need to be re-litigated or re-evaluated on an ongoing basis, even when there is precedent addressing the same AI tool.

kp.k: Algorithmic contestability presents a predicted due-process challenge
kp.d: The opinion predicts due-process difficulties because litigants cannot question algorithms and the learning AI acquires over time. It places this concern within a broader obligation to understand AI’s legal, regulatory, ethical and access challenges.
qs: Due process will be a challenge when dealing with AI tools, as a litigant cannot question the algorithms and the deep learning the AI tool acquires over time.

Judges must not only understand the legal, regulatory, ethical, and access challenges associated with AI, but they will need to continually evaluate how they or parties before them are using AI technology tools in their own docket.

kp.k: Oversight spans administrative tools and consequential risk assessments
kp.d: The opinion recommends continual review of judges’ and parties’ AI use across docket management, courtroom transcription and risk assessments affecting sentencing, pretrial release or bond, probation and parole. It also requires understanding the science and law of electronically stored information and e-discovery, and expressly distinguishes AI informing a judicial decision from AI deciding.
qs: This could include the use of basic docket management and courtroom tools (AI transcribing tools) and risk assessment tools (in making decisions on sentencing, pretrial release/bond conditions, probation, and parole).
Judges must also understand the science and law relating to electronically stored information and e-discovery.
Judicial use of AI must distinguish between using an AI application to decide and using AI to inform a decision.

kp.k: Judges should document reasoning and ensure lawful AI use
kp.d: The opinion recommends ongoing ethical assessment of each tool’s risks and benefits and placing the court’s reasoning on the record. Its conclusion requires reasonable steps to ensure that AI tools informing judicial judgment are used properly within applicable law and court rules, connecting continuing technological competence to efficiency and quality of justice.
qs: The most important thing courts can do today is to ask the right questions and place their analysis and application of how they reached their conclusion on the record.

Judicial officers have an ethical obligation to understand technology, including artificial intelligence, and take reasonable steps to ensure that AI tools on which their judgment will be based are used properly and that the AI tools are utilized within the confines of the law and court rules.
Further, as AI rapidly advances, judicial officers have an ethical duty to maintain technological competence and understand AI’s ethical implications to ensure efficiency and quality of justice.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The State Bar of Michigan Judicial Ethics Committee states that increasing AI use makes continuing technological competence and oversight an ethical obligation for judicial officers.
pts.d: In Opinion JI-155, the Committee interprets Michigan judicial conduct requirements as obliging judges to understand AI's benefits, risks and effects on judicial decisions and administration. This extends to tools used by court staff and lawyers appearing before them. Judges must take reasonable steps to ensure proper, lawful use and distinguish AI informing a decision from AI deciding.

pts.k: The Committee claims that biased algorithms or training data can influence judicial judgment and implicate fairness and impartiality duties.
pts.d: The opinion presents this as a conditional risk, not a measured finding about particular judicial tools. AI may weight factors in legally or socially inappropriate ways, and its output may fail to reflect norms or precedent.

pts.k: The Committee describes incorrect AI-generated filings as creating a need for human verification and prompting court-specific disclosure and certification requirements.
pts.d: The opinion reports that some courts require attorney review, notice of AI use and confirmation of accuracy; others additionally require confidentiality certifications and identification of AI-generated sections. These are examples of existing court responses, not a declaration that all courts impose the same requirements.

pts.k: The Committee states that properly used AI can assist legal drafting, research and docket management.
pts.d: The claimed benefits are accurate pleadings and summaries, more efficient docket management and research, and algorithm-based answers. The opinion supplies no quantified productivity estimates or performance benchmarks and conditions these benefits on proper use.

pts.k: The Committee predicts that advancing and changing AI will generate adjudication, potentially require renewed scrutiny despite precedent, and challenge due process.
pts.d: The opinion states that most AI programs continue learning and reasons that changes with additional data may require ongoing re-litigation or re-evaluation of the same application. It separately predicts due-process difficulties because litigants cannot question algorithms and acquired deep learning. These are the Committee's prospective claims, without empirical estimates or a specified forecast horizon.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The opinion relies on ethical rules, a litigation example, court orders and secondary authorities rather than empirical studies or benchmarks.
pts.d: The competence analysis draws on Michigan Code of Judicial Conduct Canons 2(B), 2(C), 3(A)(1) and 3(B)(1), Michigan Rule of Professional Conduct 1.1 and Ethics Opinion RI-381. The Committee cites Mata v Avianca as an example of improper AI-generated filings, not as a measured error rate. It references Texas and Illinois court requirements and Judge Stephen Vaden's order for verification, disclosure and confidentiality practices. UNESCO's ethical-dilemma examples support the bias discussion; Greenstein's article in The Judge’s Journal and ABA Resolution 112 supply additional commentary and policy authority. The opinion offers no quantitative evidence for efficiency gains or its future-litigation and due-process predictions.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The October 27, 2023 opinion identifies present duties and court responses alongside open-ended predictions requiring continuing oversight.
pts.d: Technological competence is framed as an existing obligation that continues as AI advances. Verification and certification orders are described as already occurring. Benefits depend on proper use; impartiality concerns arise where biased or unfair tools may influence judgment. Future adjudication is described as eventual, while renewed scrutiny is conditional on changes in learning applications. No numerical timeline is supplied.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The principal affected groups are judicial officers, court staff, practicing lawyers, litigants and the public.
pts.d: Judicial officers face continuing education, lawful-use and oversight responsibilities. Court staff's administrative and transcription tools fall within that oversight. Lawyers face verification and, in some courts, disclosure and certification requirements. Litigants may encounter AI-informed decisions affecting sentencing, pretrial release, probation or parole, as well as due-process difficulties. Public confidence, impartial treatment and quality of justice are central concerns. The opinion does not predict law-firm staffing, pricing or legal-market restructuring.
